task: set up a new device through its companion app or on-device flow: a new phone (setup, account sign-in, data transfer), a router or mesh Wi-Fi via its app, a smartwatch pairing, or a smart-home device (camera, plug, speaker, doorbell): the unbox-to-working arc — pair or connect, sign in, configure the essentials; complete when the device shows working/connected in the app or the phone reaches its fully set-up home screen. Surface pinned: the setup flow itself — not unboxing-only or review videos.

tree.label: Set up a new device
tree.note: do 1, then 2. phone routes then do 3 and 4, where 4.3 is the whole of 4. accessory routes do 4 first, then 2.5 to 2.8, then 3 - the app will not look for a device until it knows the account. then 5 where anything is carried over; uSN0 and DT4C's first pass skip it outright. then 6. 7 always, and 7.9 when 7 comes back wrong. 8 on the transfer routes, reaching into 1.10 where the erase is actually run (aawv). 9 where the device has services to configure - fok5 and NZzD do parts of it inside 6, u--l does all of it after 7.

children.label: Prepare the devices
children.note: 1.1 to 1.3 on boxed hardware only (NZzD, u--l, fok5, 9yTg); 1.4 when the hardware will not enter setup mode (9yTg). 1.5 and 1.6 on the devices being replaced, in any order. 1.7 first on the new device, and 1.10 when the answer is wrong (mIjR, _CVz). 1.8 where a transfer will run long (aawv, CKwc). 1.9 where the route leans on a backup - CKwc and _CVz satisfy it by reading a timestamp instead of running one. 1.10 also serves goal 8: the same erase, at the other end of the task.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might select a transfer method that does not align with where your most recent or complete backup is actually stored.
questions.check: Which transfer options does the page offer, and what does it say about each?
questions.say_example: How should your stuff come over? Straight from the old phone takes about twenty-five minutes. From the cloud backup, the old phone stays usable meanwhile. Or start clean. Which way?

questions.question: Which device backup do you want to restore?
questions.why: The screen lists multiple previous device backups with timestamps, requiring you to identify the correct source device to ensure your current data transfers over.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might select an outdated backup or skip the restore entirely, leaving your new phone without your expected apps and personal data.
questions.check: Which backups does the page list, with which dates and devices?
questions.say_example: Three backups here. The newest is from this morning, off your old phone. That's the one I'm restoring.

questions.question: Does the page say the selected number's transfer is not supported?
questions.why: The screen lists your available phone numbers for transfer but warns that the transfer is not supported for the selected number.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to proceed with the unsupported transfer attempt or skip it to contact your carrier directly.
questions.check: Does the page say the transfer is not supported for the selected number?
questions.say_example: It says your number can't move this way. The carrier has to do it. I'll finish the rest and leave you a note to call them.

questions.question: Which of these cellular plans are currently active?
questions.why: Identifying the active plans among the multiple listed options ensures you only transfer the lines you actually use to the new device.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to filter out old trial or inactive plans, which an agent might blindly transfer to the new device.
questions.check: Which plans does the page mark as active?
questions.say_example: Two plans were listed and only the Magenta one is active. I moved just that one.

questions.question: Which specific data categories do you want to restore from your backup?
questions.why: The screen lists categories like apps, contacts, and messages to restore, which directly impacts how much storage is used on the new device.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent decide means losing the ability to filter out unwanted apps or data from the backup, potentially cluttering the new device.
questions.check: Which restore toggles does the page show as on or off?
questions.say_example: Apps, messages, and photos are all ticked. I'm bringing it all, like you asked.

questions.question: Does the restore total drop by the size of the apps that were unselected?
questions.why: The screen showed the total restore size updating to reflect the 0.2 GB saved by excluding those specific apps.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the immediate feedback of seeing exactly how much storage space is saved by their specific selections.
questions.check: Does the total restore size update to match the deselections?
questions.say_example: Restore size tracked the deselections, from 3.4 down to 3.2 GB.

questions.question: How do you adjust the data transfer selection if your old device's backup is larger than the new device's total storage capacity?
questions.why: Users frequently buy new phones with less or equal storage but have bloated backups, triggering an 'insufficient storage' error that forces them to manually deselect photos, videos, or large apps.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might blindly attempt the full transfer and fail, or arbitrarily delete data to make it fit, rather than letting the user prioritize which personal files to keep.
questions.check: Does the page show a not-enough-storage error for the restore?
questions.say_example: The backup is bigger than the new phone can hold, so something has to stay behind. Videos are the big chunk. Leave those in the cloud and bring everything else?

questions.question: Should you use the settings from your old phone or customize them?
questions.why: The screen offers to automatically apply your previous settings or let you customize them, determining if your new phone behaves exactly like the old one.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to review and update your privacy, location, and system preferences for the new device.
questions.check: Does the page offer applying the previous settings automatically?
questions.say_example: It can copy all your old settings in one go. That's what you wanted, so I took the express path.

questions.question: Are you ready to start transferring data from your previous iPhone?
questions.why: The screen estimates the transfer will take 5 to 10 minutes, so you must decide if you have time to wait now or prefer other options.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to postpone the transfer if you need your phone immediately or prefer setting it up as a new device.
questions.check: What does the page estimate the transfer will take?
questions.say_example: Starting the copy now. It says five to ten minutes. Both phones stay on their chargers and near each other till it's done.

questions.question: What should you wait for on the new iPhone after the old device says the transfer is complete?
questions.why: The old iPhone indicates the transfer is done, but the new iPhone still needs to process the data, restart with a progress bar, and display the 'Hello' screen before you can proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the visual reassurance of seeing the new device successfully reboot and reach the welcome screen after the data handoff.
questions.check: Does the page say the new device still restarts and processes after the old one finishes?
questions.say_example: Old phone said done; new one restarted and worked through its progress bar after

questions.question: Is the visual progress bar actually moving, or has it been frozen despite the time estimate remaining unchanged?
questions.why: Setup transfers and network configurations frequently hang, and waiting indefinitely for a frozen process prevents you from taking action to force-restart it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent reading the text '1 minute remaining' won't realize the visual progress bar has been stuck at 99% for ten minutes, requiring human intuition to abort and retry.
questions.check: Has the progress bar stayed at the same point well past the estimate?
questions.say_example: The bar hasn't moved in twenty minutes. That's stuck, not slow. I'm restarting the transfer. Nothing is lost, it starts over.

children.label: Work through the setup screens
children.note: 6.1 to 6.10 in whatever order the vendor's wizard asks - no keeper reorders them and none sees all of them. 6.1 and 6.2 are what split the corpus: c_gv accepts through both, DT4C declines through both, uSN0 does one of each. 6.8 and 6.9 only on the eSIM route. 6.11 ends it. c_gv and DT4C run this whole goal twice on the same phone, and Apple Pay and Siri get asked in both passes.

questions.question: Do you notice the contradiction between the app's claim and the OS prompt regarding local network access?
questions.why: The Nighthawk app explicitly claims it 'will not access other devices on your network', but the subsequent iOS system prompt requests permission to 'find and connect to devices on your local network'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent clicking 'OK' blindly misses the fact that the app's privacy claim directly contradicts the OS-level permission it actually requests.
questions.check: Does the app's promise about network access contradict the permission it then asks for?
questions.say_example: The app promised it won't touch other devices on your network, then asked the phone for exactly that. I allowed it for setup, but the two don't match. That's worth knowing.

questions.question: Do you want to use the pre-filled first and last name for your profile?
questions.why: The screen states that Alexa will use this name to get to know you better, which determines how the assistant will address you.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose a specific nickname or preferred name for the voice assistant to use.
questions.check: Does the pre-filled name match the person's?
questions.say_example: It filled in the name from the old account. That's your ex-roommate's, not yours. Fixing it before the assistant starts calling you that.

questions.question: Should you grant the app access to your contacts and allow notifications?
questions.why: The screen explains that uploading contacts helps you connect with family and friends, but granting these system-level permissions directly impacts your data privacy and device interruptions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically allow or deny these permissions, bypassing your personal boundaries regarding data privacy and notification preferences.
questions.check: Is the app asking for a permission the setup doesn't need?
questions.say_example: It's asking for your contacts. Setup doesn't need that, so I said not now. If you use it for calling later, it'll ask again.

questions.question: Is the automatically detected date, time, and time zone correct?
questions.why: The screen showed the detected time zone as Eastern Standard Time, which needed to be verified and adjusted to the correct local time zone.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might accept an incorrect default time zone, leading to wrong timestamps on messages, alarms, or scheduled events.
questions.check: Does the detected time zone match where the person is?
questions.say_example: The phone thinks it's on Eastern time. You're Pacific. I fixed it, or every alarm would ring three hours early.

questions.question: Which launcher do you want to set as your default home screen?
questions.why: The screen prompts you to choose between Pixel Launcher and Nova Launcher as your home app and decide whether to apply this choice permanently or just once.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to stick with the custom launcher transferred from your old phone or use the new device's default interface.
questions.check: Which home-screen apps does the page offer?
questions.say_example: Kept the standard launcher as the home screen

questions.question: Which Siri voice do you prefer?
questions.why: The setup screen offers four distinct voice options or a randomized choice to configure how the assistant sounds.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means you lose the ability to personalize the daily auditory experience of interacting with your virtual assistant.
questions.check: Which voice options does the page offer?
questions.say_example: Kept the default assistant voice. Four others are available in settings.

questions.question: Which age range should I select for the person who will use this device?
questions.why: This determines which parental controls and safety features the device will automatically set up.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might apply the wrong safety restrictions or parental controls for the actual user.
questions.check: Does the page ask an age range that switches parental controls on?
questions.say_example: It asks the age of whoever uses this. That's what flips the kid safety settings on. This one's yours, so I said adult.

questions.question: Are your personal health details correct for accurate fitness tracking?
questions.why: The screen states that providing accurate details like height and weight ensures your fitness data is calculated correctly without being shared with Apple.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might skip this screen or enter default values, resulting in inaccurate calorie and activity tracking for your specific body metrics.
questions.check: Do the height and weight on the page match the person's?
questions.say_example: It guessed a height and weight for the fitness math, and they're not yours. Give me the real ones and I'll fix it. It stays on the device.

questions.question: Should you toggle the wheelchair setting on or off for activity tracking?
questions.why: The screen explicitly notes that turning on the wheelchair setting changes the fitness tracking algorithm to count pushes instead of steps.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might leave this at the default setting, resulting in completely inaccurate activity tracking if your physical mobility requires the alternative algorithm.
questions.check: Does the page offer the wheelchair activity-tracking option?
questions.say_example: There's a setting that counts pushes instead of steps for wheelchair users. Want it on? It changes how all the activity numbers work.

questions.question: Should you install the available software update now or defer it to speed up the setup?
questions.why: The screen offers a choice between "Update Now" to immediately apply important bug fixes and "Update Later" to finish the setup process faster.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent decides whether to prioritize immediate system stability or a faster initial setup time.
questions.check: Does the page offer installing the update now versus later?
questions.say_example: There's an optional update waiting. I set it to run tonight on its own so we can keep going now.

questions.question: Should you apply the required firmware update now?
questions.why: The screen states that updating from version 1.0.2.72 to 1.0.2.82 is required to ensure you have the latest security updates and bug fixes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose visibility into the specific firmware version being installed on your new router.
questions.check: Does the page say the update is required before the device works?
questions.say_example: The router needs a firmware update before anything else works. I'm starting it. It takes about ten minutes, and don't unplug it in the middle.

children.label: Set the device locks
children.note: 6.1.1 or 6.1.5 - a lock or a refusal. 6.1.2 only where the passcode is weak enough to be challenged. 6.1.3 then 6.1.4 where a biometric is enrolled. DT4C does both: defers the biometric and still has to set a passcode.

questions.question: Do you want to set up the face or fingerprint unlock now, or add it later?
questions.why: This determines whether you configure biometric authentication immediately to unlock the phone and make purchases, or skip it to save time during the initial setup.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent cannot physically scan your face, so delegating this step means you lose the ability to configure biometric security during the initial setup.
questions.check: Does the page offer biometric setup with a skip or later option?
questions.say_example: It offers face unlock. That takes your face at the camera for a minute. I can't do it for you. Now, or skip and add it later? Skipping is fine.

questions.question: Should you set up security questions for admin password recovery?
questions.why: The screen prompts you to select and answer two personal questions to ensure you can recover your admin password if you forget it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might skip the setup or choose security answers you do not know, potentially leaving you unable to recover a forgotten password.
questions.check: Does the page require choosing recovery questions?
questions.say_example: It wants two recovery questions in case the password's forgotten. Pick answers only you'd know. I'll read you the question choices.

questions.question: Does this second entry exactly match the six-digit passcode I just created?
questions.why: The screen requires you to re-enter the six digits to confirm your new passcode and prevent accidental lockouts from typos.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means sharing your primary device unlock code with an agent, compromising your personal security.
questions.check: Does the page accept the second entry of the passcode?
questions.say_example: Passcode confirmed on the second entry

questions.question: What lock screen PIN do you want to set?
questions.why: The screen requires a 4 to 16 digit PIN and warns that forgetting it will force a factory reset that erases all your data.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent choose the PIN means you will not know the code to unlock your own device, risking a total loss of your data.
questions.check: Does the page ask to create a passcode, and what does it warn about forgetting it?
questions.say_example: Time to pick the unlock code. It's yours alone. I shouldn't know it. It warns that forgetting it means a full erase, so pick one you'll keep. Type it when ready.

questions.question: Do you want to disable the 'Prevent Weak Password' requirement?
questions.why: The admin password setup screen includes a toggle to prevent weak passwords, which is on by default, meaning you must decide whether to enforce strict password rules or allow a simpler, potentially less secure password.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might leave the toggle on and generate a complex password you cannot remember, or turn it off and set a weak password that compromises your router's security.
questions.check: Is the prevent-weak-password toggle on by default?
questions.say_example: Left the weak-password block on for the router admin

questions.question: Do you want to use the easily guessed passcode anyway or change it to a stronger one?
questions.why: The screen warns that this passcode protects access to your iPhone and iCloud data, meaning a weak passcode lowers your overall security.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might choose to use the weak passcode to speed up the setup process, leaving your personal device and data vulnerable.
questions.check: Does the page warn the chosen passcode is easily guessed?
questions.say_example: The phone says that code is easy to guess, and it guards everything on here. Want to pick a different one? Your call. I'll go with either.

questions.question: Did your first Face ID scan finish?
questions.why: The screen confirms the first scan is complete, which is necessary before you can proceed to the second scan to finish biometric setup.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the physical agency to position their own face and ensure their biometric security is configured accurately.
questions.check: Does the page confirm the first scan finished?
questions.say_example: First face scan done, second one followed

questions.question: Should you rename this fingerprint or accept the default?
questions.why: The screen confirms the fingerprint is enrolled and offers the option to rename it from the default "Fingerprint ID 1" or just tap "OK" to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to give the fingerprint a memorable custom name instead of the generic default.
questions.check: Does the page offer renaming the enrolled fingerprint?
questions.say_example: Kept the default name on the enrolled fingerprint

children.label: Answer the consent screens
children.note: 6.2.1 always. the rest as the vendor asks: Google runs 6.2.2, 6.2.4 and 6.2.5 as one block (kB3r, fok5), Apple asks 6.2.3 twice on the same phone (DT4C). 6.2.6 only in NZzD, where it is pre-checked and never discussed.

questions.question: Do you agree to the terms and conditions?
questions.why: The screen presents the mandatory legal agreements required to use the iOS device.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to read and understand the specific legal terms and privacy policies you are consenting to.
questions.check: Which agreements does the page require accepting before setup continues?
questions.say_example: It won't go further without agreeing to the terms. They're the standard ones for using the device. I don't agree to legal things for you. OK to accept?

questions.question: Do you accept the Google Terms of Service and the binding arbitration agreement?
questions.why: Proceeding requires agreeing to Google's legal terms, which includes a binding individual arbitration agreement that affects how disputes are resolved.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally review the specific legal terms and privacy policies you are being bound to before proceeding.
questions.check: Do the terms include a binding arbitration clause?
questions.say_example: These terms include giving up the right to sue in court. Disputes go to an arbitrator instead. There's no opt-out except not using the device. Still OK?

questions.question: Do you want to keep Google Drive backup enabled for this account?
questions.why: Turning off the backup toggle triggers a warning that the existing device backup for your account will be permanently deleted from Google Drive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means an agent might permanently delete your existing cloud backup or sync your data to the wrong account without your consent.
questions.check: Does the page warn that switching backup off deletes the existing backup?
questions.say_example: Switching backup off here would delete the old phone's backup from the cloud. I'm leaving it on.

questions.question: Do you want to share your usage data with the maker?
questions.why: This determines whether your device sends background usage data to help Apple improve its products and services.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to enforce your personal privacy boundaries regarding background data collection.
questions.check: Is the page asking to send usage or diagnostic data to the maker?
questions.say_example: It asks to send usage data back to the maker. That's optional, so I said no.

questions.question: Do you want to set up a voice profile now?
questions.why: Creating a voice profile allows Alexa to recognize you and personalize responses, but requires agreeing to store your voice data in the cloud.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent cannot speak with your actual voice to train the profile, meaning this specific personalization step must be skipped or done manually by you.
questions.check: Does the page say the voice profile stores your voice with the account?
questions.say_example: It offers to learn your voice so it knows it's you asking. In exchange, your voice gets stored with the account. Want it, or skip?

questions.question: Do you want to share your Siri audio recordings with Apple?
questions.why: This choice determines whether Apple is allowed to store your audio interactions with Siri, which directly impacts your privacy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over your privacy preferences regarding whether your voice recordings are stored and shared with Apple.
questions.check: Is the page asking to keep voice recordings for company review?
questions.say_example: It asks to keep your voice recordings for people at the company to review. That's optional. I said no.

questions.question: Should you add your phone number to your Google account?
questions.why: This determines whether Google can use your number for features like video calls and personalized ads, which involves occasional SMS verification.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent decide means you lose control over whether your personal phone number is shared with Google for advertising and communication services.
questions.check: Does the page say the number would be used for ads as well as security?
questions.say_example: Skipped adding your number to the account. The number would be used for ads as well as account recovery.

questions.question: Do you want to enable Amazon Sidewalk to share your device's approximate location?
questions.why: This setting applies to all your linked Echo and Ring devices and shares your approximate location to help neighbors find connected items, which directly impacts your privacy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically opt you into this community network, sharing your location data and bandwidth without your explicit consent.
questions.check: Does the page say the setting shares data and applies to all linked devices?
questions.say_example: It asks to switch on Sidewalk, which shares a slice of your internet and rough location with neighbors' devices. It'd be on for every Echo you own. I said no.

questions.question: Should you enable location services?
questions.why: This determines whether apps like Maps and Find My are allowed to gather and use data about your approximate location.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent make this choice means you lose direct control over your personal privacy and location tracking preferences.
questions.check: Is the page asking to turn location on, and what does it say needs it?
questions.say_example: It asks to turn location on. Maps and finding a lost phone need it, so I said yes. Each app still asks you separately after this.

questions.question: Do you want to use this new device as your primary source for sharing your location?
questions.why: The setup flow prompts you to decide whether to switch your Find My and Messages location sharing from your previous device to this new one.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might incorrectly configure which of your devices broadcasts your physical location to friends and family.
questions.check: Does the page offer moving location sharing from the old device to this one?
questions.say_example: Moved your location sharing over to the new phone

questions.question: What is your Wi-Fi password, and do you want to save it to Amazon?
questions.why: The screen requires the Wi-Fi password to connect the device and includes a checked-by-default option to save this password to Amazon.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might automatically save your Wi-Fi password to Amazon's servers without giving you the chance to opt out for privacy.
questions.check: Is the save-password-to-the-company box checked by default?
questions.say_example: The password box came with 'save to Amazon' already ticked. I unticked it. The Wi-Fi password stays on your own devices.

questions.question: Do you want to set up the optional extras now, or get a reminder to finish later?
questions.why: The screen offers the choice to either complete the setup for optional features immediately or postpone them with a reminder.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether they want to invest time right now to configure optional features or defer them until later.
questions.check: Does the page offer optional extras with a skip or later option?
questions.say_example: There's a pile of optional extras here, like the assistant, payments, and screen time. I'm skipping them all so the phone's ready sooner. They wait in settings whenever you want one.

questions.question: Do you want to add the suggested credit card to Apple Pay now or skip it?
questions.why: The screen prompts you to verify a card on file by entering its security code, but provides an option to skip this step and add it later.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically skip this step or lack the security code to verify the card, leaving you without Apple Pay configured or requiring you to finish the financial setup manually.
questions.check: Is the page asking to add or verify a payment card?
questions.say_example: It suggests adding your card for tap-to-pay. I skipped it. Anything with your card needs you anyway, and it's two minutes in settings later.

questions.question: Do you want to invite shared users to access this device?
questions.why: The app prompts you to give friends and family access to your Ring devices to share security responsibilities.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to immediately grant device access to family members who might need to monitor the security system.
questions.check: Does the page offer giving other people access to the device?
questions.say_example: Skipped the shared-user invites. Who sees the cameras is your call.

questions.question: Do you want to enable Smart Alerts despite the potential delay in notifications?
questions.why: The screen offers Smart Alerts for better event filtering, but warns that the extra video processing can delay motion alerts by several seconds.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means losing the ability to weigh the trade-off between receiving highly relevant alerts and getting them instantly.
questions.check: Does the page warn the smarter alerts arrive a few seconds late?
questions.say_example: Left smart alerts on. That means fewer false alarms, but a few seconds slower.

questions.question: Do you want to adjust the motion detection sensitivity?
questions.why: The screen explains that moving the slider changes how many motion alerts you receive and how many events the device captures.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means losing the ability to tailor the alert frequency to your specific environment, potentially leading to missed events or notification spam.
questions.check: Where does the page put the sensitivity slider and what is it set to?
questions.say_example: Left motion sensitivity at the middle default

questions.question: Do you want future system updates to install on their own?
questions.why: The screen offers to install future iOS updates automatically for security and new features, but you might prefer to review and install them manually.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to manually control when their device undergoes potentially disruptive software updates.
questions.check: Does the page offer automatic versus manual future updates?
questions.say_example: I set updates to install on their own overnight. That's the safest default. You can flip it to manual in settings any time.

questions.question: Is there a hidden 'Skip' or 'No Thanks' option to bypass the premium subscription trial during account creation?
questions.why: Many smart home apps disguise a premium subscription trial as a mandatory setup step, hoping users will enter a credit card and forget to cancel.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically enter payment details to get past the screen, inadvertently committing the user to a recurring financial charge for a service they don't want.
questions.check: Does the page have a skip or no-thanks besides the trial button?
questions.say_example: This page pushes the paid plan hard, but there's a small maybe-later at the bottom. Taking that.

questions.question: Do you want the paid iCloud storage upgrade the page is offering?
questions.why: The screen warns that you are almost out of your free 5 GB of storage and offers a paid monthly subscription to ensure your photos, documents, and backups remain safe.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically accept the upgrade to ensure successful backups, committing you to an unwanted recurring monthly charge.
questions.check: What monthly price and storage does the offer show?
questions.say_example: You're nearly out of free storage, and it's offering 50 gigabytes for 99 cents a month. That's a recurring charge, so it's your call. Want it, or should I clear space instead?

questions.question: Does the 'free trial' for the premium service require entering a credit card that will automatically be charged when the trial ends?
questions.why: Manufacturers often gate features behind subscriptions (like Ring Protect or eero Secure) and use the setup flow to secure a payment method for an auto-renewing trap.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent click through the trial screens means you might unwittingly agree to a recurring monthly charge that you have to remember to cancel later.
questions.check: Does the trial ask for a card and say it charges when the trial ends?
questions.say_example: The free month wants a card and starts billing itself when the month ends. I skipped it. If you ever want the trial, we set a reminder to cancel first.

questions.question: Do you want to opt in to marketing emails and survey invites from Google?
questions.why: The final setup screen includes a checkbox to receive updates on features, offers, and surveys from Google Hardware.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over whether your email address is subscribed to promotional communications and product surveys.
questions.check: Is there a marketing-email checkbox, and is it pre-ticked?
questions.say_example: There's a box for marketing emails on the last screen. I left it unticked.

questions.question: Do you prefer a light or dark visual theme for the interface?
questions.why: This determines the overall visual style of the interface, and the screen allows you to preview how the display adjusts to either option before confirming.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually preview the themes and select the aesthetic that best suits your personal preference.
questions.check: Which theme is selected on the page?
questions.say_example: Kept the default light theme. Dark is one toggle away.

questions.question: Do you prefer standard or zoomed display scaling?
questions.why: Zoomed makes text and controls larger for easier reading, while standard fits more content on the screen at once.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually preview both options and select the interface size that best matches your eyesight and usability preferences.
questions.check: Which display scale is selected on the page?
questions.say_example: Kept standard display scaling

questions.question: Do you want to adjust the watch's text size and boldness now, or leave it at the default?
questions.why: The screen provides a bold text toggle and a size slider to customize your reading experience, along with an option to defer the choice.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent cannot see the real-time preview on your physical watch to judge which text size and weight is most comfortable for your eyes.
questions.check: What text size and boldness does the page show selected?
questions.say_example: Kept the default text size. Bold and bigger are in settings.

questions.question: Do you want to keep the Always On Display enabled for your watch?
questions.why: This determines if your watch screen remains visible when your wrist is down and how it handles sensitive information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to decide your personal preference for screen visibility and privacy.
questions.check: Is the always-on display shown as on or off?
questions.say_example: Left the always-on display on. It dims but stays readable.

questions.question: Do you prefer the Grid or List view for your apps?
questions.why: The setup flow lets you choose between a Grid or List layout for navigating your watch apps.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to select the app navigation style that best fits your visual preferences.
questions.check: Which app view is selected on the page?
questions.say_example: Kept the grid view for watch apps

questions.question: Do you want to use True Tone Display?
questions.why: This determines whether your screen will automatically adapt to ambient lighting conditions to make colors appear consistent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to visually preview the difference and choose your preferred screen color temperature.
questions.check: Is True Tone shown as on or off?
